ann_115.text: Through this part, capital gains clearly lower a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less slowly at first, then faster, from about 58% at none to about 9% at $6,849, flattening out near the bottom because it cannot go much lower.
The drop is slightly smaller for the 49 people born in Portugal (about 58% to about 12%).
Being born in Portugal on its own slightly raises the predicted chance through this part (it stays at about 58%).

ann_116.text: Through this part, being older clearly lowers a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less steadily up to about 34 years, then no further: from about 90% at 22 years to about 56% at 58 years.
Working as a handler or cleaner raises it to about 77% (on the training data only).
The drop with age is slightly larger for handlers or cleaners (about 98% to about 65%) than for other occupations (about 90% to about 56%).

ann_117.text: Through this part, compared with the occupations it does not tell apart (which include a professional specialty), farming or fishing clearly raises a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less to about 79%, and executive or managerial jobs (about 41%) and sales jobs (about 53%) clearly lower it.
A doctorate clearly lowers it to about 51%.
Being born in Colombia raises it to above 99% (on the training data only).
Being born in Colombia clearly raises it, and even more so without a doctorate: from about 58% to above 99%, against about 51% to above 99% with a doctorate.

Working in the armed forces raises it, and even more so with a doctorate: from about 51% to about 67% with a doctorate, against about 58% to about 67% otherwise; the model has little data on this (only 12 people in the armed forces).
Unpaid work raises it to about 73% (17 people, on the training data only), and working in the armed forces on its own raises it only slightly (12 people); the model has little data on this.

ann_118.text: Through this part, being of any race other than White raises a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 58% to about 65% (on the training data only).

ann_119.text: Through this part, other service jobs clearly raise a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 58% to about 77%.
Being Asian or Pacific Islander lowers it to about 46%, and an 11th-grade education raises it to about 66% (on the training data only).
Being born in Hungary lowers it to about 51%, but the model has little data on this (16 people), on the training data only.
A 10th-grade education (about 54%), a vocational associate degree (about 56%) and a 7th-8th grade education (about 59%) change it only slightly (on the training data only).
Working as a machine operator or inspector slightly raises it, to about 60%.

ann_120.text: Through this part, any marital status other than being married clearly raises a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 58% to about 94%, and being married to a member of the armed forces clearly lowers it to about 39%.

Compared with a husband, the model clearly gives someone's own child (about 86%) and other relatives (about 65%) a higher chance, and wives (about 32%), people not in a family (about 47%) and people listed as unmarried (about 52%) a lower one.
Being a woman clearly raises it to about 73%.

ann_121.text: Through this part, a higher education level, capital losses and longer working hours clearly lower a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less steadily: from about 73% at 7 to about 42% at 13 on the 1-16 education scale, from about 58% at no losses to about 28% at $1,887, and from about 67% at 24 hours a week to about 49% at 55.
A higher census sampling weight slightly lowers it steadily, from about 60% at 66,572 to about 55% at 328,216 (on the training data only).

ann_122.text: Through this part, compared with a professional specialty, private household service (above 99%), a missing occupation (about 86%), transport or moving (about 70%) and the occupations this part does not tell apart (about 67%) clearly raise a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less.

Compared with a high-school education, preschool (about 82%) and 9th grade (about 63%) clearly raise it, and a professional school degree (about 40%), a master's degree (about 48%) and a bachelor's degree (about 51%) clearly lower it; a race recorded as 'other' clearly lowers it to about 53%.

Compared with being born in the United States, being born in Trinidad and Tobago (about 97%), 'South' (as recorded, about 84%), Vietnam (about 82%), Peru (about 81%), the Dominican Republic or China (about 79%), Mexico (about 75%), Nicaragua (about 74%), the outlying US territories (about 73%), Ecuador or El Salvador (about 70%), Haiti (about 68%), Guatemala (about 67%) or Greece (about 66%) raises it (on the training data only).

Compared with private-sector work, self-employment without incorporation raises it to about 71%, and federal government work (about 45%) and a missing work class (about 46%) lower it (on the training data only).
Never having worked raises it to about 68%, but the model has little data on this (9 people), on the training data only.
Some college (about 54%), being American Indian or Eskimo (about 61%) and an academic associate degree (about 58%) change it only slightly.

ann_123.text: For a typical person, the model clearly lowers the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less with capital gains slowly at first, then faster (about 58% at none to 9% at $6,849, flattening out near the bottom because it cannot go much lower), and with age steadily up to about 34 years, then no further (about 90% at 22 years to 56% at 58).

ann_115.original: Capital-gain term (exit idn_capgain, added to the output logit): f = -2.49*cg - 2.32*relu(0.576*cg - 0.0522*nc32 - 0.274), inputs z-scored. For the 91.6% of train rows with zero capital gain (cg_z=-0.146) the gate is off and f=+0.36. The ReLU 1690 opens at cg_z=0.476 (5.2% of rows), steepening the slope from -2.49 to -3.83 per SD: a monotone one-knot piecewise-linear decrease in logit P(<=50K). Any substantial gain forces a >50K prediction (f=-5.7 at cg_z=1.66, -50 at the max). native-country:32 (Portugal, 51 rows) shifts the knot to cg_z~3.0 for those rows only. Evidence: line plot on the full train split (39,073 rows) gives corr(cg, f)=-0.999; ablation (term replaced by its train mean) drops train accuracy 0.854->0.838 and AUC 0.910->0.892 and flips 8.1% of predictions, the largest nonlinear term. Category names (in parentheses) are inferred from PMLB's alphabetical label encoding and checked against category frequency and P(<=50K) on train; the network sees only the index. Output class 1 is income <=50K (train base rate 0.761), so negative terms push toward >50K.
ann_115.proposed: More capital gains lower the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less, slightly less so for people born in Portugal.

ann_116.original: Youth gate (exit idn_age): f = -0.0624*age + 0.669*relu(-2.95*age + 0.395*occ6 - 0.861). ReLU 2682 is active when age_z < -0.32 (43% of train rows, younger than about the median age), where it raises logit P(<=50K) linearly as age falls, reaching +2.58 at the youngest. Above the threshold only the small direct term (-0.062 per SD) remains. occupation:6 (Handlers-cleaners, 4.3% of rows) moves the threshold to age_z < 0.34: an age x occupation interaction in which handlers-cleaners count as 'young' up to an older age. Evidence: heatmap of age x occupation:6 on full train (39,073 rows); ablation flips 5.2% of predictions, accuracy 0.854->0.849, AUC 0.910->0.903. Category names (in parentheses) are inferred from PMLB's alphabetical label encoding and checked against category frequency and P(<=50K) on train; the network sees only the index. Output class 1 is income <=50K (train base rate 0.761), so negative terms push toward >50K.
ann_116.proposed: Older age lowers the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less, slightly more so for handlers or cleaners, who also get a higher chance overall.

ann_117.original: Hub ReLU 350 plus direct occupation/workclass terms (exit idn_hub350). Every input is a one-hot, so on the data the subgraph is a lookup table over 16 observed category combinations. 7974 (occupation:4 only) and the 10971->3077 chain (native-country:4 only) are single-input relays. With none of the seven categories set, 350=1.21 and f=+0.33. Each of occupation:4 (Exec-managerial), occupation:5 (Farming-fishing), occupation:2 (Armed-Forces), education:10 (Doctorate) and workclass:8 (Without-pay) turns 350 off; the direct weights then set the category value: Exec-managerial f=-0.35, Doctorate +0.04, Farming-fishing +1.33, Without-pay +1.03, Armed-Forces +0.34, Sales (occupation:12) +0.12 with 350 still on. native-country:4 (Columbia, 64 rows, 98% <=50K) drives 350 to ~43.5 and f to +10.4, a hard-coded 'Columbia => <=50K' rule. So the hub works as an off-switch shared by several high- or low-income categories, plus one memorised country rule. Evidence: per-combination enumeration on full train; sensitivity on train (largest: native-country:4 0.34, occupation:4 0.23); ablation flips 2.5% of predictions, AUC 0.910->0.906. Category names (in parentheses) are inferred from PMLB's alphabetical label encoding and checked against category frequency and P(<=50K) on train; the network sees only the index. Output class 1 is income <=50K (train base rate 0.761), so negative terms push toward >50K.
ann_117.proposed: An occupation and education lookup: farming raises, and executive or managerial jobs, sales jobs and a doctorate lower, the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less; being born in Colombia raises it, less so with a doctorate.

As a function of one binary input it takes two values: +0.649 for White and +0.962 for non-White, so being White lowers logit P(<=50K) by 0.31. ann_118.proposed: Being of any race other than White raises the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less.

ann_119.original: Single-category ReLU units on one-hot inputs, with their direct edges. Exits: idn_gatedcats (summed term), 10878 (race:1 chain) and 7734 (native-country:18); all three feed the output logit with weights 1, -0.115 and -0.0056. Each unit sees one binary input, so on the data it is two-valued and exactly affine in that input. 5330 and 10607 are always active (linear); 1339 is active only for occupation:8; 12248->10878 only for race:1; 7734 only for native-country:18. Evidence: sensitivity on full train (occupation:8 dominates at 0.30); ablation flips 1.2% of predictions, AUC 0.910->0.909. Output class 1 is income <=50K (train base rate 0.761), so negative terms push toward >50K.
ann_119.proposed: Other service jobs and an 11th-grade education raise the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less, and being Asian or Pacific Islander lowers it; other categories here change it only slightly.

ann_120.original: Purely linear household block (exit idn_household): marital-status, relationship and sex one-hots. On-vs-off logit effects: marital-status:1 (Married-AF-spouse) -3.15, relationship:5 (Wife) -2.59, marital-status:2 (Married-civ-spouse) -2.39, relationship:1 (Not-in-family) -1.95, relationship:4 (Unmarried) -1.78, relationship:0 (Husband) -1.52, relationship:2 (Other-relative) -1.24, sex=Male -0.67. relationship:3 (Own-child) has no edge, so it is the reference category with the highest P(<=50K). ann_120.proposed: The household part: not being married, being someone's own child or another relative, and being a woman raise the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less; being a wife, married to a member of the armed forces, not in a family or listed as unmarried lowers it compared with a husband.

ann_121.proposed: A higher education level, capital losses and longer hours lower the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less; the census sampling weight lowers it slightly.

ann_122.original: Linear one-hot offsets (exit idn_catlinear) for the remaining workclass, education, occupation, race and native-country categories. Inputs are z-scored one-hots, so a rare category gets a large on-value and a small weight becomes a large effect. ann_123.proposed: Capital gains and losses, older age, a higher education level, longer hours, marriage, being a wife and executive jobs lower the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less; a marital status other than married, being someone's own child, a woman, and service, farming or manual jobs raise it.

summary.text: For a typical person (a 37-year-old White man married to a civilian spouse, born in the United States, a high-school graduate in a professional specialty job in the private sector, working 40 hours a week with no capital gains or losses), capital gains clearly lower the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less slowly at first, then faster, from about 58% at none to about 9% at $6,849, flattening out near the bottom because it cannot go much lower.
Being older clearly lowers it steadily up to about 34 years, then no further: from about 90% at 22 years to about 56% at 58 years.

Any marital status other than being married clearly raises it to about 94%, and the model clearly gives someone's own child in the household a higher chance (about 86%) and a wife a lower one (about 32%) than a husband.
Compared with a professional specialty, private household service (above 99%, 187 people), a missing occupation (about 86%) and farming or fishing (about 85%) clearly raise it.

A higher education level, capital losses and longer working hours clearly lower it steadily (from about 73% at 7 to about 42% at 13 on the 1-16 education scale, to about 28% at $1,887 of losses, and from about 67% at 24 hours a week to about 49% at 55), and being a woman clearly raises it to about 73%.
Being born in Colombia (64 people) raises the predicted chance to above 99% (on the training data only).

The ReLU 1690 opens at cg_z=0.476 (5.2% of rows), steepening the slope from -2.49 to -3.83 per SD: a monotone one-knot piecewise-linear decrease in logit P(<=50K). Any substantial gain forces a >50K prediction (f=-5.7 at cg_z=1.66, -50 at the max). native-country:32 (Portugal, 51 rows) shifts the knot to cg_z~3.0 for those rows only. Evidence: line plot on the full train split (39,073 rows) gives corr(cg, f)=-0.999; ablation (term replaced by its train mean) drops train accuracy 0.854->0.838 and AUC 0.910->0.892 and flips 8.1% of predictions, the largest nonlinear term. Category names (in parentheses) are inferred from PMLB's alphabetical label encoding and checked against category frequency and P(<=50K) on train; the network sees only the index. Output class 1 is income <=50K (train base rate 0.761), so negative terms push toward >50K.

parts.name: household_linear
parts.original_hypothesis: Purely linear household block (exit idn_household): marital-status, relationship and sex one-hots. On-vs-off logit effects: marital-status:1 (Married-AF-spouse) -3.15, relationship:5 (Wife) -2.59, marital-status:2 (Married-civ-spouse) -2.39, relationship:1 (Not-in-family) -1.95, relationship:4 (Unmarried) -1.78, relationship:0 (Husband) -1.52, relationship:2 (Other-relative) -1.24, sex=Male -0.67. relationship:3 (Own-child) has no edge, so it is the reference category with the highest P(<=50K). A married husband gets -1.52-2.39-0.67 relative to an unmarried female own-child. Evidence: sensitivity on full train equals |weights|; ablation is the largest of all children: accuracy 0.854->0.815, AUC 0.910->0.853, 13.3% of predictions flip. Category names (in parentheses) are inferred from PMLB's alphabetical label encoding and checked against category frequency and P(<=50K) on train; the network sees only the index. Output class 1 is income <=50K (train base rate 0.761), so negative terms push toward >50K.

parts.name: age_youth_gate
parts.original_hypothesis: Youth gate (exit idn_age): f = -0.0624*age + 0.669*relu(-2.95*age + 0.395*occ6 - 0.861). ReLU 2682 is active when age_z < -0.32 (43% of train rows, younger than about the median age), where it raises logit P(<=50K) linearly as age falls, reaching +2.58 at the youngest. Above the threshold only the small direct term (-0.062 per SD) remains. occupation:6 (Handlers-cleaners, 4.3% of rows) moves the threshold to age_z < 0.34: an age x occupation interaction in which handlers-cleaners count as 'young' up to an older age. Evidence: heatmap of age x occupation:6 on full train (39,073 rows); ablation flips 5.2% of predictions, accuracy 0.854->0.849, AUC 0.910->0.903. Category names (in parentheses) are inferred from PMLB's alphabetical label encoding and checked against category frequency and P(<=50K) on train; the network sees only the index. Output class 1 is income <=50K (train base rate 0.761), so negative terms push toward >50K.

parts.name: numeric_linear

More schooling, longer hours and capital losses (a proxy for owning assets) all push toward >50K. There are no hidden units. Evidence: sensitivity on full train matches the weights; ablation: accuracy 0.854->0.839, AUC 0.910->0.893, 7.0% of predictions flip. Category names (in parentheses) are inferred from PMLB's alphabetical label encoding and checked against category frequency and P(<=50K) on train; the network sees only the index. parts.name: category_linear
parts.original_hypothesis: Linear one-hot offsets (exit idn_catlinear) for the remaining workclass, education, occupation, race and native-country categories. Inputs are z-scored one-hots, so a rare category gets a large on-value and a small weight becomes a large effect. On-vs-off logit effects: occupation:9 (Priv-house-serv) +6.27, native-country:38 (Trinadad&Tobago) +3.23, native-country:35 (South) +1.32, native-country:40 (Vietnam) +1.23, education:13 (Preschool) +1.16, native-country:29 (Peru) +1.15, occupation:0 (unknown) +1.06, education:14 (Prof-school) -0.72. Most are rare low-income categories, memorised as offsets. Evidence: sensitivity on full train equals |weights|; ablation flips 3.2% of predictions, AUC 0.910->0.905. Category names (in parentheses) are inferred from PMLB's alphabetical label encoding and checked against category frequency and P(<=50K) on train; the network sees only the index. Output class 1 is income <=50K (train base rate 0.761), so negative terms push toward >50K.

parts.name: occupation_hub_350
parts.original_hypothesis: Hub ReLU 350 plus direct occupation/workclass terms (exit idn_hub350). Every input is a one-hot, so on the data the subgraph is a lookup table over 16 observed category combinations. 7974 (occupation:4 only) and the 10971->3077 chain (native-country:4 only) are single-input relays. With none of the seven categories set, 350=1.21 and f=+0.33. Each of occupation:4 (Exec-managerial), occupation:5 (Farming-fishing), occupation:2 (Armed-Forces), education:10 (Doctorate) and workclass:8 (Without-pay) turns 350 off; the direct weights then set the category value: Exec-managerial f=-0.35, Doctorate +0.04, Farming-fishing +1.33, Without-pay +1.03, Armed-Forces +0.34, Sales (occupation:12) +0.12 with 350 still on. native-country:4 (Columbia, 64 rows, 98% <=50K) drives 350 to ~43.5 and f to +10.4, a hard-coded 'Columbia => <=50K' rule. So the hub works as an off-switch shared by several high- or low-income categories, plus one memorised country rule. Evidence: per-combination enumeration on full train; sensitivity on train (largest: native-country:4 0.34, occupation:4 0.23); ablation flips 2.5% of predictions, AUC 0.910->0.906. Category names (in parentheses) are inferred from PMLB's alphabetical label encoding and checked against category frequency and P(<=50K) on train; the network sees only the index. Output class 1 is income <=50K (train base rate 0.761), so negative terms push toward >50K.

parts.name: gated_category_offsets
parts.original_hypothesis: Single-category ReLU units on one-hot inputs, with their direct edges. Exits: idn_gatedcats (summed term), 10878 (race:1 chain) and 7734 (native-country:18); all three feed the output logit with weights 1, -0.115 and -0.0056. Each unit sees one binary input, so on the data it is two-valued and exactly affine in that input. 5330 and 10607 are always active (linear); 1339 is active only for occupation:8; 12248->10878 only for race:1; 7734 only for native-country:18. The one real interaction is 3845 (education:0, education:8, occupation:7): it switches off for occupation:7 (Machine-op-inspct), which removes the tiny education:0/8 effects for machine operators. On-vs-off logit effects on train: occupation:8 (Other-service) +0.91, education:1 (11th) +0.46, race:1 (Asian-Pac-Islander) -0.44, native-country:18 (Hungary, 16 rows) -0.31, education:5 (7th-8th) +0.12, education:8 (Assoc-voc) -0.12, education:0 (10th) -0.06, occupation:7 -0.02. Evidence: sensitivity on full train (occupation:8 dominates at 0.30); ablation flips 1.2% of predictions, AUC 0.910->0.909. Category names (in parentheses) are inferred from PMLB's alphabetical label encoding and checked against category frequency and P(<=50K) on train; the network sees only the index. Output class 1 is income <=50K (train base rate 0.761), so negative terms push toward >50K.

parts.name: race_white_effect
parts.original_hypothesis: race:4 (White, 85.5% of rows) term (exit idn_white): f = -0.395*r4 + 0.761*relu(1.41*r4 + 1.40*relu(0.617*r4 - 0.185) + 0.388). As a function of one binary input it takes two values: +0.649 for White and +0.962 for non-White, so being White lowers logit P(<=50K) by 0.31. The two-ReLU chain (7193->771) is excess structure for a single offset. Evidence: line plot on full train (two observed points, corr -1.0); ablation is negligible (AUC 0.9099->0.9096, 0.66% of predictions flip). Category names (in parentheses) are inferred from PMLB's alphabetical label encoding and checked against category frequency and P(<=50K) on train; the network sees only the index. Output class 1 is income <=50K (train base rate 0.761), so negative terms push toward >50K.

reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

settings.effect_scale: log-odds (output pre-activation) for verification; predicted risk for the typical patient for wording
